note: You should increase your following distance whenever conditions make it harder to see, stop, or react in time. This includes following large vehicles that block your view, following motorcycles or other vulnerable road users, driving in bad weather or heavy traffic, exiting expressways, or when someone is tailgating you. More space gives you extra time to avoid collisions.

question: If an approaching driver doesn’t dim their high beams, where should you look?
options: a: Toward the left side of the road.,b: At the wheels of the approaching vehicle.,c: Toward the right side of the road.
note: When an oncoming driver does not dim their high beams, the bright light can temporarily blind you. To protect your night vision and still stay in your lane, briefly glance toward the right side of the road, using the right edge line or curb as a guide, rather than looking directly into the headlights.

question: What should you do when the driver behind you wants to pass?
options: a: Speed up.,b: Maintain your speed or slightly slow down to help them pass safely.,c: Slow down sharply to allow room for the pass.
note: If another driver wants to pass you, you should help them do it safely. Maintain a steady speed or slightly reduce your speed so they can pass without having to speed excessively or cut back in too closely. Never speed up when someone is trying to pass.

question: How can road rage and aggressive driving be reduced?
options: a: Use proper turn signals.,b: Allow extra travel time.,c: Obey speed limits.,d: All of the above.
note: Planning ahead and allowing extra travel time is one of the most effective ways to reduce road rage, because you are less likely to feel rushed or frustrated. Using turn signals and obeying speed limits are also important courteous and safe driving habits that help prevent conflicts with other drivers.

question: When faced with an oncoming car and a bicyclist, what should you do?
options: a: Pull onto the shoulder.,b: Split the difference.,c: Let the car pass, then pass the bike.
note: When you meet an oncoming car and a bicyclist at the same time, you should not try to squeeze between them. Let the oncoming vehicle pass first, then move over safely to pass the bicyclist when you have enough space and no oncoming traffic. This reduces risk by dealing with only one hazard at a time.

question: When driving near a motorcycle, you must:
options: a: Allow the motorcycle a full lane.,b: Drive on the shoulder beside it.,c: Allow the motorcycle half a lane.
note: Motorcycles are entitled to use an entire traffic lane, just like a car. You must not crowd them or share the lane side‑by‑side, because they need space to maneuver, avoid hazards, and maintain balance.

question: How long should you signal before changing directions?
options: a: At least 75 feet.,b: At least 100 feet.,c: At least 50 feet.
note: You should signal for at least 100 feet before turning or changing direction so other road users have enough time to see and react to your movement. At higher speeds, such as on highways, many states also recommend signaling for a longer distance to maintain safety.

question: What is the first thing to adjust when getting into a car to drive?
options: a: Seat belt.,b: Steering wheel.,c: Seat position.
note: Adjust the seat first so you can reach the pedals and controls comfortably and see clearly out of the windows. Once the seat is set, adjust the steering wheel and mirrors, and then fasten your seat belt so it fits correctly across your shoulder and lap.

question: How should you check for vehicles in your blind spots before changing lanes?
options: a: Quickly turn your head to check blind spots.,b: Adjust rearview mirrors every few minutes.,c: Honk your horn before turning.
note: Before changing lanes, quickly glance over your shoulder in the direction you plan to move to check your blind spot. Mirrors do not show everything, so this head check helps you see vehicles that may be hidden just beside your car.

question: To prevent drowsiness on long trips, you should:
options: a: Slow down.,b: Stop regularly for rest.,c: Turn on the radio.
note: On long trips, plan to stop regularly to get out, walk around, and rest. Short breaks help prevent drowsiness much more effectively than just slowing down or turning on the radio.

question: Before starting the ignition, you should:
options: a: Ensure only child passengers are buckled.,b: Ensure only adult passengers are buckled.,c: Ensure all passengers are buckled.
note: Before starting the vehicle, ensure all passengers, regardless of age, have their seat belts buckled.

question: What is the safest way to drive in traffic?
options: a: Fluctuate speed to stay alert.,b: Drive faster than traffic flow.,c: Drive with the flow of traffic.
note: The safest approach in traffic is to move with the general flow while staying within the posted speed limit. Large speed differences between you and surrounding traffic increase the risk of collisions, whether you are going much faster or much slower.

question: What should you assume when passing a recently parked vehicle?
options: a: The driver will open the door.,b: Speed up.,c: Slam on brakes.
note: When passing a recently parked vehicle, you should assume someone might open a door or pull out suddenly. Slow slightly if needed and leave extra space so you can safely avoid a door or sudden movement into your lane.

question: What is the most important thing to remember about speed management in curves?
options: a: Drive at the posted speed limit, then slow at the curve’s sharpest part.,b: Slow down before entering the curve.,c: Accelerate gently before the curve.
note: You should always slow down before you enter a curve. Braking while already in the curve can cause you to lose traction because your tires are trying to both turn and slow down at the same time. Enter the curve at a safe speed, then maintain a steady speed and only accelerate gently as you begin to straighten out.

question: What are the strategies to avoid a collision?
options: a: Stop, turn, or speed up.,b: Move into the other vehicle’s lane.,c: Stay in your lane and brace for impact.
note: To avoid a collision, you may need to brake to stop, steer around the hazard, or speed up briefly to get out of danger, depending on the situation. Using these options early and smoothly gives you more space and time to avoid a crash.

question: What should you do if driving in another driver’s blind spot?
options: a: Stay in the blind spot.,b: Keep a steady pace.,c: Move forward or drop back to be visible.
note: Blind spots are areas a driver cannot see with mirrors alone. If you are traveling in another driver’s blind spot, move forward or drop back so you are clearly visible in their mirrors, reducing the risk of being hit if they change lanes.

question: What is defensive driving?
options: a: Following closely behind another vehicle.,b: Getting ahead of poor drivers.,c: Identifying and avoiding dangerous situations.
note: Defensive driving means staying alert, scanning the road, anticipating what other drivers might do, and adjusting your speed or position to avoid potential collisions before they happen.

question: Why is signaling your intentions important?
options: a: Only necessary during the maneuver.,b: Required by law and a good habit.,c: Only needed if other traffic is present.
note: Signaling is required by law and helps other road users predict what you will do. You must signal well before turning, changing lanes, or pulling away from the curb—typically at least 100 feet in advance in many states—so others have time to react safely.

question: What defines a good defensive driver?
options: a: Always drives at a constant speed.,b: Anticipates other drivers’ actions.,c: Drives slowly at all times.
note: A good defensive driver constantly scans the road, anticipates what other drivers, pedestrians, and cyclists might do, and adjusts speed and position early to avoid trouble. Defensive driving is about awareness and anticipation, not just driving slowly or at one constant speed.

question: What should you do on slippery roads?
options: a: Use alternate routes.,b: Drive as on dry roads.,c: Increase following distance.
note: On slippery roads, it takes longer to stop, so you should increase your following distance. Leaving more space between you and the vehicle ahead gives you extra time to brake gently and avoid skidding.

question: What is a blind spot?
options: a: Area you can’t see without moving your head.,b: Directly behind your vehicle.,c: Area seen in your rearview mirror.
note: A blind spot is any area around your vehicle that you cannot see in your mirrors and must turn your head to check. These are usually along the sides and slightly to the rear of your vehicle, and sometimes directly behind large vehicles.

question: What is required if a flagger is directing traffic in a construction zone?
options: a: Follow the flagger’s directions.,b: Assume the flagger isn’t authorized to direct traffic.,c: Follow surrounding traffic despite the flagger’s instructions.
note: Flaggers in construction zones are authorized to direct traffic and their instructions have the same legal force as traffic signals or signs. You must follow their directions, slow down, and drive carefully to protect workers and other drivers.

question: What can cause distracted driving?
options: a: Changing a radio station or CD.,b: Eating, drinking, or smoking.,c: Talking or texting on a cell phone.,d: All of the above.
note: Distracted driving can be caused by many activities, including changing the radio or CD, eating, drinking, smoking, and talking or texting on a cell phone. Any task that takes your eyes off the road, your hands off the wheel, or your mind off driving increases your crash risk.

question: How should you drive on slippery roads?
options: a: Drive the speed limit cautiously.,b: Drive faster.,c: Slow down.
note: On slippery roads from rain, snow, or ice, you must slow down—often well below the posted speed limit. The speed limit is the maximum under ideal conditions, not a target. Reducing speed gives you more time to react and helps prevent skids.

question: What is checking your blind spot before changing lanes or merging?
options: a: A bad driving habit.,b: Unnecessary.,c: A good driving habit.
note: Checking your blind spot by quickly looking over your shoulder before changing lanes or merging is an essential safety habit. Mirrors do not show everything, so a shoulder check helps you see vehicles, motorcycles, or bicycles that might be hidden from view.

question: Why are railroad crossings considered dangerous?
options: a: Trains can stop quickly, so crossings are low risk.,b: They are hazardous because trains cannot stop quickly.,c: They’re safe parking spots.
note: Railroad crossings are dangerous because trains are large, fast, and cannot stop quickly. Always slow down, look and listen for trains, obey all warning signs and signals, and never stop on the tracks. Cross only when you are sure the tracks are clear and you can fully clear the crossing.

question: What typically causes hydroplaning?
options: a: Sudden turns.,b: Excessive stops.,c: High speeds on wet roads.
note: Hydroplaning happens when a layer of water builds up between your tires and the road so the tires lose contact and you slide. This is most likely at higher speeds on wet roads, especially with worn tires or standing water.

question: How should you handle a tailgater?
options: a: Slam on your brakes.,b: Speed up to create distance.,c: Slow down or change lanes to let them pass.
note: When someone is following too closely, the safest response is to create a safe situation for yourself and let them go by. Gradually slow down or change lanes when it is safe so the tailgater can pass. Never brake suddenly or speed up, as that increases the risk of a crash.

question: What should a small vehicle driver be prepared for when passing a large vehicle?
options: a: Loud noises.,b: Excess air pollution.,c: Wind gusts from the large vehicle.
note: When passing a large vehicle such as a truck or bus, be prepared for strong wind gusts that can push or pull your smaller vehicle sideways. You may need to make small steering corrections to stay in your lane. While noise or exhaust may be noticeable, the main safety concern is the air turbulence created by the large vehicle.

question: What should you do at a railroad crossing without flashing signals or gates?
options: a: Cross quickly.,b: Always stop.,c: Prepare to yield to any train.
note: At a railroad crossing without active signals or gates, you must slow, look, and listen for trains and be prepared to stop. Cross only when you are sure no train is coming and there is enough room to clear the tracks completely without stopping on them.

question: How should you take turns on slick roads?
options: a: Take turns more slowly.,b: Change lanes quickly.,c: Accelerate quickly.
note: On slick or icy roads, you should slow down before and during turns. Taking turns more slowly reduces the chance of your tires losing traction and helps you keep control of the vehicle through the curve.

question: Which activity increases the risk of a crash for distracted drivers?
options: a: Using a CD player.,b: Using a cell phone.,c: Using the radio.
note: Using a cell phone while driving greatly increases crash risk because it takes your attention away from the road and often your eyes and hands as well. Even hands‑free calls can distract your mind from driving.

question: When should you honk your horn?
options: a: Traveling through an intersection.,b: Passing a bicyclist.,c: To warn a child running into the street.
note: The horn is a warning device, not for routine use. You should use it to alert others to a danger they may not see, such as a child running into the street, so they can stop or move out of the way in time.

question: How should you use a freeway exit ramp correctly?
options: a: Slow down before entering the exit ramp.,b: Slow down once on the exit ramp.,c: Keep speed constant on the exit ramp.
note: On freeways, maintain your speed until you are actually on the exit ramp so you do not disrupt traffic behind you. Once you are on the ramp, use the ramp’s deceleration area to slow to the posted exit speed safely.

question: What should you ensure when passing on a multilane highway?
options: a: The passing lane is clear.,b: Pass only on the right.,c: Watch for oncoming traffic.
note: On a multilane highway, always make sure the lane you will use to pass is clear before moving over. Check mirrors and blind spots, signal, then change lanes smoothly. After passing, return to your original lane only when you can see the entire front of the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror. Passing is usually done on the left; passing on the right is allowed only in specific, clearly safe situations where it is legal.

question: What factors do vehicle stopping distances not depend on?
options: a: Reaction time.,b: Time of day.,c: Brake condition.
note: Stopping distance is made up of your reaction distance and your braking distance. It depends on how quickly you react, your speed, road and weather conditions, and the condition of your brakes and tires. The time of day by itself does not change how far it takes a vehicle to stop.

question: What must you do if a transit vehicle signals to re-enter the main roadway?
options: a: Honk to alert the driver.,b: Yield to the transit vehicle.,c: Move to the left lane.
note: When a bus or transit vehicle signals that it is pulling back into the lane from a stop, you must yield. This means you should let the vehicle re-enter by changing lanes if safe, or by slowing or stopping so it can merge without forcing it to brake or swerve.

question: Where should you look to reduce headlight glare at night?
options: a: Straight ahead.,b: Over your shoulder.,c: To the right side of the road.
note: At night, oncoming headlights can temporarily blind you if you stare at them. To reduce glare, briefly glance toward the right edge of your lane and use the road edge or lane line as a guide while still keeping track of the road ahead.

question: What should you do when approaching a railroad crossing warning sign?
options: a: Drive faster than the train.,b: Be prepared to stop if a train is nearby.,c: Go around lowered gates.
note: When you see a railroad crossing warning sign, slow down, look and listen for trains, and be prepared to stop if a train is approaching. Never try to beat a train, and never drive around or under lowered gates or ignore flashing lights.

question: What is the most effective way to reduce injury or death risk in a traffic crash?
options: a: Wear your seat belt.,b: Drive only on weekdays.,c: Stay in the right lane on multilane highways.
note: Wearing a seat belt every time you drive or ride in a vehicle is the single most effective way to reduce the risk of serious injury or death in a crash. Seat belts keep you inside the vehicle, spread crash forces over stronger parts of your body, and work with airbags and other safety systems.

question: When a pedestrian crosses in front of your vehicle, you should:
options: a: Speed up to pass them.,b: Flash your lights.,c: Slow down.
note: Drivers must slow down and be prepared to stop whenever a pedestrian is crossing in front of them. You must always yield to pedestrians in crosswalks and use extra caution around children or in areas where people may step into the road unexpectedly.

question: What affects braking distance?
options: a: The condition of the pavement.,b: The speed of your vehicle.,c: The condition of your brakes and tires.,d: All of the above.
note: Braking distance is the distance your vehicle travels after you apply the brakes until it stops. It increases with higher speed and is also affected by the condition of your brakes and tires and by the road surface. Worn brakes or tires and wet, icy, or loose pavement all make your vehicle take longer to stop.

question: Is texting while driving legal in Washington State?
options: a: Legal but not recommended.,b: A safe activity.,c: Illegal.
note: In Washington State, it is illegal to text while driving. Texting takes your eyes, hands, and attention away from the road, greatly increasing crash risk, so the law prohibits it and you can be cited if you do it.

question: How do worn or bald tires affect driving?
options: a: Make turning and steering more difficult.,b: Increase the risk of hydroplaning.,c: Increase stopping distance.,d: All of the above.
note: Worn or bald tires greatly reduce traction. This increases your stopping distance, makes it harder to steer and turn—especially in wet or emergency situations—and raises the risk of hydroplaning because the tire cannot channel water away effectively. Replacing worn tires is essential for safe handling and braking.

question: What do your brake lights indicate to other drivers?
options: a: You’re making a turn.,b: Your emergency brake is on.,c: You’re slowing or stopping.
note: Brake lights warn drivers behind you that you are slowing down or stopping. This gives them time to ease off the accelerator or brake so they don’t rear-end your vehicle.

question: Which statement is true about passing a motorcycle?
options: a: Following closely is okay.,b: A motorcycle with two riders is more balanced.,c: Change lanes completely when passing.
note: Motorcycles are entitled to a full lane, just like cars. When you pass a motorcycle, you must move completely into the adjacent lane and pass as you would another car. Never crowd or share the lane with a motorcycle, and avoid following too closely because they can stop and maneuver more quickly than larger vehicles.

question: What should you expect when driving through an area where children are playing?
options: a: Children know when to cross.,b: Children stop at the curb.,c: Children may run out without looking.
note: In areas where children are playing, assume they may suddenly run into the street without looking. Slow down, cover the brake, and be prepared to stop quickly, because children are unpredictable and may not follow traffic rules.

question: How do trucks compare to smaller vehicles in stopping distance?
options: a: Trucks need longer distances to stop.,b: Trucks need less time to pass on downgrades.,c: Trucks have a smaller turning radius.
note: Large trucks are much heavier than passenger cars, so they need more distance to come to a complete stop, especially at higher speeds or when loaded. You should avoid cutting closely in front of trucks because they cannot stop as quickly as smaller vehicles.

question: What should you avoid when changing lanes?
options: a: Failing to check your side and rearview mirrors before moving.,b: Signaling your intentions before changing lanes.,c: Checking for other drivers who may be moving into the same lane.
note: You should never change lanes without checking your mirrors and blind spot, and signaling your intention. Failing to check mirrors means you may not see vehicles approaching quickly from behind or alongside you, which can lead to a sideswipe or rear-end collision.

question: What should you do when changing lanes on a highway?
options: a: Signal, check mirrors, and check your blind spot before moving.,b: Signal only if traffic is heavy.,c: Change lanes if you do not see a vehicle directly beside you.
note: A safe lane change requires three steps together: signal well in advance to let others know your intention, check your mirrors to see traffic behind and beside you, and quickly glance over your shoulder to check your blind spot. Only move into the new lane when you are sure it is clear.

question: Why do larger vehicles have larger blind spots?
options: a: They have no blind spots.,b: Their size creates larger blind spots.,c: They have smaller blind spots.
note: Larger vehicles such as trucks, buses, and SUVs sit higher and have more body length and width, which creates bigger areas around them that the driver cannot see in mirrors. These larger blind spots, especially directly behind and along the sides, mean other drivers should avoid lingering where the larger vehicle’s driver cannot easily see them.

question: After stopping for a school bus unloading children:
options: a: Accelerate quickly.,b: Watch for children walking along the road.,c: Wait for children to wave before proceeding.
note: When a school bus is stopped with red lights flashing and stop arm extended, you must stop and remain stopped. After the lights stop flashing and the stop arm is withdrawn, proceed slowly and be prepared to stop again. Children may walk along or cross the road unexpectedly, so you must watch carefully and drive with extra caution.

question: Before changing lanes on a multilane highway, you should:
options: a: Turn on your headlights.,b: Sound your horn.,c: Check your mirrors and blind spots.
note: Before changing lanes, signal, check your mirrors, and then look over your shoulder to check your blind spot in the direction you plan to move. Mirrors alone do not show vehicles in your blind spots, so a quick head check is essential to be sure the lane is clear before you move over.

question: What should you do if the driver ahead is distracted, driving with one hand and talking?
options: a: Give them extra space.,b: Know they’re reducing safety.,c: Avoid following their example.
note: A distracted driver is more likely to make sudden or unpredictable moves. By giving them extra space, you create a safety buffer so you have more time and room to react if they drift, brake suddenly, or miss a traffic signal.

question: How can you prevent hydroplaning?
options: a: Ensure good tire tread depth.,b: Ensure proper tire inflation.,c: Reduce speed in rain.
note: Hydroplaning happens when your tires ride on top of water instead of gripping the road. You reduce this risk by slowing down in rain, and by having good tread and proper tire pressure so the tires can channel water away.

question: How does driving at night compare to driving during the day?
options: a: No more or less dangerous.,b: More dangerous.,c: Less dangerous.
note: Driving at night is more dangerous because you can see less of the road, it is harder to judge distance and speed, glare from headlights can temporarily blind you, and there is a higher chance of encountering fatigued or impaired drivers.

question: Which is true when passing another vehicle?
options: a: Signal before moving into the passing lane.,b: Check mirrors and blind spot.,c: Wait until both headlights are visible in rearview.,d: All of the above.
note: Before passing another vehicle, you must signal your intention, check your mirrors and your blind spot to be sure the lane is clear, and after passing, do not move back into the lane until you can see the entire front of the passed vehicle, including both headlights, in your rearview mirror. All three steps are required for a safe pass.

question: Why is night driving more challenging?
options: a: Cars overheat more at night.,b: Visibility is reduced.,c: Rain is more likely at night.
note: Night driving is more difficult because you cannot see as far or as clearly, even with headlights. Reduced visibility makes it harder to spot hazards in time, so you should use proper headlights, reduce your speed, and make sure you can stop within the distance you can see ahead.

question: Why is following another car too closely dangerous?
options: a: You may not see the vehicle’s turn signals.,b: You may not see the road between cars.,c: You may not have time to stop if the vehicle ahead slows or stops.
note: Following too closely, or tailgating, is dangerous because you may not have enough time or space to stop if the vehicle ahead slows or stops suddenly. Keeping a safe following distance gives you room to react and brake smoothly, reducing the chance of a rear‑end collision.

question: What determines the space needed to cross traffic?
options: a: Use of turn signals.,b: Road, weather, and oncoming traffic conditions.,c: Presence of a stop sign.
note: The time and space you need to safely cross traffic depend mainly on how fast other vehicles are coming, how far away they are, and how road and weather conditions affect traction and visibility. You must judge gaps based on these conditions so you can clear the intersection without forcing others to slow or stop.

question: How should you change lanes from the left to the right lane?
options: a: Check mirrors, signal, and look over your right shoulder.,b: Look in mirrors only.,c: Check rearview mirror only.
note: Before changing lanes to the right, check your mirrors, signal, and then look over your right shoulder to check your blind spot. Only move when the lane is clear and you can change lanes smoothly and safely.

question: When exiting a highway, when should you slow down?
options: a: On the main road before the exit lane.,b: At a toll booth.,c: In the exit lane.
note: Maintain highway speed on the main roadway so you do not disrupt traffic. Begin slowing only after you are fully in the exit or deceleration lane, then reduce speed to match the ramp’s safe speed and any posted advisory signs.

question: How should you drive at night?
options: a: Use high beams when no oncoming vehicles.,b: Wear sunglasses to reduce glare.,c: Use high beams in rain.
note: At night, use your high beams on open roads when there are no oncoming vehicles or vehicles close ahead of you, and dim them when other traffic is present. Headlights must be on from 30 minutes after sunset to 30 minutes before sunrise and any time visibility is poor.

question: Which statement about winter driving is not true?
options: a: Winter is the most difficult season.,b: Check antifreeze and washer fluid.,c: Using cruise control is safe.
note: Using cruise control on snow, ice, or other slippery surfaces is unsafe because the system can apply power when the tires have poor traction, making it easier to lose control or skid. In winter, you should maintain full manual control of speed and be ready to adjust quickly to changing road conditions.

question: What is distracted driving?
options: a: Nothing to worry about.,b: Extremely risky behavior.,c: Very uncommon.
note: Distracted driving means your attention is taken away from driving by something else, such as your phone, passengers, or other activities. It is extremely risky because even a brief loss of focus can cause you to miss hazards, react too slowly, or leave your lane, putting everyone on the road in danger.

question: What should you do before changing lanes?
options: a: Rely only on your mirrors.,b: Signal only as you start moving.,c: Signal in advance, then check mirrors and blind spots before moving.
note: Before changing lanes, you must signal in advance (at least 100 feet in most areas, and about five seconds on freeways), then check your mirrors and look over your shoulder to clear your blind spot before moving.

question: What lights should you use when driving in rain?
options: a: Low beam headlights.,b: High beam headlights.,c: Parking lights.
note: In rain, always use low beam headlights so you can see and be seen. High beams can reflect off rain and make it harder to see, and parking lights alone do not provide enough visibility or signal your presence clearly to other drivers.

question: When should you signal before passing another vehicle?
options: a: Just before changing lanes.,b: After changing lanes.,c: Early enough to inform other drivers.
note: Signal early enough before passing so other drivers clearly understand your intention and have time to react. Turning on your signal only at the last moment or after you move into the next lane does not give others enough warning and can lead to unsafe lane changes.

question: What is the most important thing to remember when backing a car?
options: a: Look carefully behind and yield to vehicles and pedestrians.,b: Keep one foot on the brake while backing.,c: Rely only on the rearview mirror.
note: When backing, you must look carefully behind you and yield to pedestrians, bicyclists, and other vehicles. Turn and look through the rear window, checking all directions, and move slowly. Do not rely only on mirrors or cameras, because they can miss people or objects in blind spots.

question: Before making a turn, you should:
options: a: Increase your speed.,b: Use your turn signal.,c: Turn the wheel.
note: Before turning, you should signal well in advance—typically at least three to four seconds—so others know you plan to slow or change direction. Signaling early gives drivers and pedestrians time to adjust and helps prevent sudden, unexpected movements that can cause crashes.

question: Is using a hand-held cell phone to make a call while driving legal in Washington State?
options: a: Safer than hands-free.,b: Allowed for teenage drivers.,c: Illegal.
note: In Washington State, it is illegal to hold a cell phone in your hand while driving for calls, texting, or data use. If you must use a phone, use hands-free options and only when it is safe to do so.

question: How can you reduce the risk of hydroplaning?
options: a: Avoid speeding on wet roads.,b: Use tires with proper tread and air pressure.,c: Replace worn tires.,d: All of the above.
note: Hydroplaning happens when your tires ride on a layer of water and lose contact with the road, causing a loss of steering and braking control. You reduce this risk by driving slower on wet roads and by keeping your tires in good condition with proper tread depth and correct air pressure.

question: What should be your first response to reduced visibility?
options: a: Turn on headlights.,b: Reduce speed.,c: Turn on wipers.
note: When visibility is reduced, your first response should be to slow down so you have more time to react to hazards you may not see until later than usual. After reducing speed, you should also use headlights and wipers as needed so you can see and be seen.

question: When must your vehicle’s headlights be turned on?
options: a: 30 minutes after sunset to 30 minutes before sunrise.,b: One hour before sunset to one hour after sunrise.,c: From sunrise to sunset.
note: Headlights must be on from 30 minutes after sunset to 30 minutes before sunrise, as required by law.

question: How does stopping distance change?
options: a: Increases on wet or icy roads.,b: Increases on paved highways.,c: Increases at night.
note: Stopping distance is the total distance your vehicle travels from the moment you see a hazard until you come to a complete stop. On wet or icy roads, your tires have less traction, so it takes longer to slow down and stop. This is why you must reduce speed and increase your following distance in bad weather.

question: What should you do at an unmarked railroad crossing?
options: a: Always stop completely.,b: Slow down and be prepared to stop.,c: Assume all crossings have signals.
note: At an unmarked railroad crossing, you must slow down, look, and listen for trains, and be ready to stop. Stop if you see or hear a train or if your view is blocked, and only cross when you are sure no train is coming and there is enough space to clear the tracks safely.

question: What should you know when approaching a heavy truck from behind on a hill?
options: a: It may be slower than the speed limit.,b: You can always safely pass.,c: It’s always legal to pass.
note: Heavy trucks often climb hills much more slowly than the posted speed limit because of their weight. When you approach a truck from behind on a hill, be prepared for it to be moving slowly and avoid sudden lane changes. Passing on hills can be dangerous or illegal because of limited sight distance and no-passing zones.

question: What should you do when driving to an unfamiliar area?
options: a: Rely on road signs.,b: Plan your trip in advance.,c: Have a general idea of your destination.
note: Before driving in an unfamiliar area, plan your trip in advance. Knowing your route, major turns, and alternatives reduces last‑second lane changes, sudden stops, and distractions from trying to navigate while driving.

question: What technique helps avoid crashes in icy or snowy conditions?
options: a: Add extra vehicle weight.,b: Exit highways quickly.,c: Reduce speed.
note: Reducing speed on ice or snow gives you more time to react and shortens the distance you travel while trying to stop. You should also increase your following distance so you have extra space if you or others start to slide.

question: When should you check your blind spot?
options: a: When changing lanes.,b: When turning left or right.,c: When pulling from a curb.,d: All of the above.
note: You should check your blind spot any time you are about to move sideways or into an area you cannot see with your mirrors alone. This includes changing lanes, turning left or right, and pulling away from a curb. A quick glance over your shoulder helps you see vehicles, bicycles, or pedestrians that may be hidden in your mirrors.

question: How do you check your blind spot before changing lanes?
options: a: Look into the left side mirror.,b: Look into the right side mirror.,c: Look over your shoulder.
note: Mirrors do not show the areas directly alongside your vehicle. To check your blind spot before changing lanes, quickly look over your shoulder in the direction you plan to move to be sure no vehicle is hidden beside you.

question: How should you respond if an aggressive driver cuts you off?
options: a: Flash your lights to signal their mistake.,b: Stay calm and move out of their way.,c: Call the police immediately.
note: If an aggressive driver cuts you off, stay calm, give them space, and move out of their way when it is safe. Avoid eye contact, gestures, or actions that could escalate the situation; your priority is to prevent a crash, not to correct their behavior.

question: Why must you use extra caution near a pedestrian with a white cane?
options: a: They are deaf.,b: They are a police officer.,c: They are blind.
note: A pedestrian with a white cane or a guide dog is blind or visually impaired. You must use extra caution: slow down, yield the right‑of‑way, and be prepared to stop. Never honk or try to rush them; allow them plenty of time and space to cross safely.

question: If another driver is passing your car, you should:
options: a: Signal when it’s safe for them to pass.,b: Pull off the road.,c: Maintain a steady speed and stay in your lane while they pass.
note: When another driver is passing you, stay in your lane and maintain a steady, safe speed so they can judge the pass accurately. Do not speed up. You do not need to check for oncoming traffic for them; that is the passing driver’s responsibility. If anything, you may slightly reduce speed to make the pass easier and safer.

question: What should you do while backing?
options: a: Rely only on mirrors.,b: Flash your lights.,c: Check behind by turning your head.
note: When backing, you should turn your head and look directly through the rear window so you can clearly see what is behind you. Check around the vehicle before getting in, back up slowly, and use your mirrors only as a supplement to looking over your shoulder. This helps you spot children, pedestrians, or obstacles that mirrors might miss.

question: When should you not pass another vehicle?
options: a: When approaching an intersection.,b: When school bus lights are flashing.,c: On a hill or curve.,d: All of the above.
note: You must not pass when your view or the situation makes it unsafe, such as when approaching or in an intersection, when a school bus has flashing red lights, or on a hill or curve where you cannot see oncoming traffic. Passing in any of these situations greatly increases the chance of a head‑on or side‑impact collision.

question: What happens when drivers eat or drink while driving?
options: a: They are better drivers because they aren’t hungry.,b: They make no driving errors.,c: They have trouble controlling their vehicle.
note: Eating or drinking while driving takes at least one hand and part of your attention away from driving. This makes it harder to steer smoothly, stay in your lane, and react quickly to traffic or hazards, so you can lose control more easily.

question: Where should you look if an oncoming vehicle’s high beams are on?
options: a: The center of the road.,b: The right side of the road.,c: Either side of the road.
note: If an oncoming driver fails to dim their high beams, briefly glance toward the right edge of your lane and use it as a guide. This reduces glare, helps you avoid being blinded, and still keeps you aligned correctly in your lane.

question: What should you do while waiting to complete a left turn in an intersection?
options: a: Signal and keep wheels turned left.,b: Signal and keep wheels straight.,c: Flash headlights to clear traffic.
note: When waiting to turn left, keep your wheels straight and your turn signal on. If your wheels are turned left and you are hit from behind, your car can be pushed into oncoming traffic. With wheels straight, a rear-end collision is less likely to send you into opposing lanes.

question: What is a safe way to drive through a curve?
options: a: Slow down entering, speed up exiting.,b: Maintain constant speed.,c: Speed up entering, slow down exiting.
note: On curves, reduce speed before you enter so your tires can grip the road and you can steer smoothly. As you come out of the curve and the road straightens, you can gradually increase speed again if it is safe and within the speed limit.

question: What should you do if you are being tailgated?
options: a: Move to the right if possible.,b: If you cannot change lanes, slow down gradually.,c: Never slow down abruptly.
note: If another driver is following too closely, the safest response is to make it easy for them to pass. When there is a lane to your right and it is safe, move to the right and let the tailgater go by. If you cannot change lanes, slow down gradually to increase your following distance ahead and encourage the tailgater to pass when safe. Never brake suddenly, because that can cause a rear‑end collision.

question: How much following distance should you maintain at high speeds?
options: a: One second.,b: Four seconds.,c: Two seconds.
note: At higher speeds you need more time and space to react and stop. A minimum four‑second following distance gives you more room to brake or steer away if the vehicle ahead suddenly slows or stops.

question: Which statement about speed is true?
options: a: Driving too slowly can be dangerous.,b: Speeding can kill.,c: Speeding is safe for skilled drivers.
note: Speeding greatly increases your stopping distance and the force of any collision, which raises the chance of serious injury or death, no matter how skilled you are. Driving too slowly can also be unsafe if you block traffic, but the most clearly true and critical statement is that speeding can kill.

question: What should you do when driving in sleet or snow?
options: a: Keep windshield and mirrors clear.,b: Increase following distance.,c: Approach vehicles with caution.,d: All of the above.
note: In sleet or snow you should do all three: keep your windshield and mirrors clear so you can see, increase your following distance because stopping takes longer on slick roads, and approach other vehicles very cautiously to avoid skids and rear‑end collisions.

question: What driving technique helps conserve gasoline?
options: a: Idling in the driveway.,b: Accelerating quickly.,c: Slowing down gradually.
note: Slowing down gradually and anticipating stops helps you use less fuel. Smooth driving reduces hard braking and rapid acceleration, both of which waste gasoline by forcing the engine to work harder to get the vehicle back up to speed.

question: How does distracted driving affect a driver’s performance?
options: a: Causes the driver to drive faster.,b: Is never dangerous.,c: Slows reaction to hazards.
note: Distracted driving means your eyes, hands, or mind are not fully on driving. This delay in attention slows your reaction to sudden hazards, traffic signals, or changes in road conditions, greatly increasing the risk of a crash.

question: Why is it important to be alert to motorcycles?
options: a: They rarely use headlights.,b: They are harder to see than cars.,c: Motorcyclists are less skilled.
note: Motorcycles are smaller and narrower than cars, so they are easier to overlook in mirrors and blind spots. Their size also makes it harder to judge their speed and distance, so drivers must look carefully and check mirrors and blind spots before changing lanes or turning.

question: Which is true about driving in changing weather?
options: a: Adjust driving for sudden weather changes.,b: Slow down in rain and fog.,c: Be aware of vehicles behind in bad weather.,d: All of the above.
note: In changing weather, you must adjust your speed and driving to match visibility and road conditions. In rain, fog, snow, or ice, slowing down is essential to maintain traction and stopping distance. You should also increase following distance and stay alert for vehicles that may be traveling too fast for conditions.

question: Why should drivers be extra cautious around motorcyclists, bicyclists, and pedestrians?
options: a: They follow different traffic laws than larger vehicles.,b: They are harder to spot in traffic.,c: They always have the right-of-way.
note: Motorcycles, bicycles, and pedestrians are smaller and less visible than cars and trucks, so they can be hidden in blind spots or blend into the background. Because they are more vulnerable in a crash, drivers must look carefully for them, check mirrors and blind spots, and give them extra space.

question: If driving a slow-moving vehicle in a no-passing zone with traffic behind, you should:
options: a: Pull over if five or more vehicles are behind you.,b: Pull over if one vehicle is behind you.,c: Pull over if two or more vehicles are behind you.
note: On many two‑lane roads, if you are driving slowly in a no‑passing zone and five or more vehicles are lined up behind you, you should pull over where it is safe and let them pass. This reduces driver frustration and helps prevent risky passing maneuvers.

question: How should you handle an aggressive driver?
options: a: Avoid eye contact and let them pass.,b: Cut them off to slow them down.,c: Tailgate them.
note: With an aggressive driver, your goal is to avoid a confrontation. Stay calm, do not make eye contact or respond to their behavior, and safely slow down or change lanes so they can pass you.

question: What should you do when approaching railroad tracks?
options: a: Look, listen, slow down, and be prepared to stop.,b: Speed up to cross before gates lower.,c: Drive around lowered gates.
note: When approaching railroad tracks, you must look and listen for trains, slow down, and be prepared to stop. Never assume the tracks are clear, and never try to beat a train or go around lowered gates, because trains cannot stop quickly and a collision is usually fatal.

question: What should you do when meeting a car with blinding headlights?
options: a: Keep your bright lights on until they dim theirs.,b: Dim your lights and look toward the right edge of the road.,c: Dim your lights and speed up to pass.
note: When another driver approaches with high beams on, you should dim your own headlights to low beam and avoid looking directly into the glare by glancing toward the right edge of your lane. Briefly flashing your high beams once can be used to remind the other driver to dim their lights, but you should never leave your high beams on or speed up. Using bright lights against oncoming traffic or increasing speed when visibility is reduced is unsafe and can lead to a collision.

question: What should you do when borrowing an unfamiliar vehicle?
options: a: Assume all vehicles are the same.,b: Hide your unfamiliarity.,c: Familiarize yourself with controls.
note: Before driving an unfamiliar vehicle, take a moment to learn where and how the controls work, including lights, turn signals, wipers, gear selector, parking brake, and seat and mirror adjustments. Make sure everything works properly and correct any obvious defects before you drive so you can operate the vehicle safely in traffic and in bad weather.

question: What should you do to drive safely at night?
options: a: Increase your following distance, use lights properly, and reduce speed.,b: Avoid driving if tired and stop often to rest.,c: Ensure headlights and all vehicle lights work properly before driving at night.
note: At night, you should increase your following distance so you have more time to react with reduced visibility, avoid driving when you are tired to prevent drowsy driving, and make sure your headlights and other lights work properly so you can see and be seen.

question: How should you enter a freeway?
options: a: Signal, yield to traffic, and enter at traffic speed.,b: Signal and enter, as freeway traffic must yield.,c: Drive slowly to check traffic.
note: When entering a freeway, you must use your turn signal, look for a gap, and yield to traffic already on the freeway. Use the entrance ramp and acceleration lane to reach the speed of traffic so you can merge smoothly without forcing other drivers to brake suddenly.

question: What should a driver do if driving much slower than the speed limit?
options: a: Always claim the right-of-way.,b: Prevent following cars from passing.,c: Pull off the road to let others pass.
note: If you are driving much slower than the normal flow of traffic and vehicles are stacking up behind you, you should safely pull off the road or into a turnout area to let others pass. This reduces the risk of unsafe passing and keeps traffic flowing smoothly.

question: Which statement about railroad crossings is true?
options: a: Illegal to go around lowered gates.,b: Stop when directed by a flagger.,c: Not all crossings have signals or gates.
note: You must never drive around or under lowered railroad gates; it is illegal and extremely dangerous. Always stop when a flagger, signal, or gate indicates a train is coming, and remember that some crossings have no lights or gates, so you must look and listen carefully before crossing.

question: What should you do when making a left turn at a green light?
options: a: Yield to oncoming traffic and turn when safe.,b: Turn quickly ahead of oncoming traffic.,c: Signal others to stop so you can turn.
note: A green light does not give you the right‑of‑way for a left turn across oncoming traffic. You must yield to oncoming vehicles and pedestrians in the crosswalk, then turn only when there is a safe gap and no signs or signals prohibiting the turn.

question: What should you do when driving near a blind pedestrian with a white cane or guide dog?
options: a: Slow down and be prepared to stop.,b: Take the right-of-way.,c: Proceed normally.
note: When you see a blind pedestrian with a white cane or guide dog, you must slow down, yield the right-of-way, and be prepared to stop. Blind pedestrians rely on sound and right-of-way laws to cross safely, so give them extra time and space.

question: What ensures safety when backing your vehicle?
options: a: Honk before shifting to reverse.,b: Check behind before entering the vehicle.,c: Check rearview mirrors.
note: Before backing, you should walk behind your vehicle to check for children, pedestrians, or objects that may be in your blind spots. Mirrors alone cannot show everything directly behind the vehicle, especially small children or low objects, so physically checking the area first is an important safety step.

question: How should you approach a railroad crossing with a crossbuck but no gates or lights?
options: a: Cross with extreme caution when no train is coming.,b: Turn down radio to hear trains.,c: Wait for a flagger’s clearance.
note: A crossbuck marks the location of a railroad crossing and means you must yield to trains. When there are no gates or flashing lights, slow down, look and listen carefully in both directions, and be prepared to stop. Cross only when you are sure no train is coming and there is enough space to clear the tracks completely without stopping on them. Obey any flagger if one is present.

question: What is the most common cause of traffic crashes?
options: a: New drivers.,b: Human error.,c: Bad weather.
note: Most traffic crashes are caused by human error, such as inattention, distraction, misjudging another vehicle’s speed or distance, or making sudden, unsafe maneuvers. While bad weather and road conditions can contribute, driver decisions and mistakes are the primary cause of most collisions.

question: How can you relieve fatigue on a long trip?
options: a: Stop and rest every two hours.,b: Do arm exercises every hour.,c: Drive with one eye open.
note: On long trips, fatigue slows your reaction time and makes it harder to pay attention. Stopping every couple of hours to get out, walk, stretch, or take a short nap in a safe place helps you stay alert and reduces the risk of drowsy‑driving crashes.

question: What should you do if an intersection is blocked by traffic?
options: a: Go slowly until traffic moves.,b: Get close to the car in front.,c: Stay out of the intersection.
note: If traffic is backed up and you cannot fully clear the intersection, you must stay out of the intersection, even if the light is green. Entering and stopping in the intersection blocks cross traffic and can cause gridlock and citations.

question: Why is a space cushion around your vehicle important?
options: a: Keeps traffic moving at a safe pace.,b: Prevents distractions from other vehicles.,c: Gives you time to react to unexpected situations.
note: A space cushion is the open area around your vehicle that gives you time and room to react if another driver brakes suddenly, swerves, or makes a mistake. By not following too closely and keeping space on the sides when possible, you can brake, steer, or change lanes more safely to avoid a collision.

question: How should you prepare for potential road hazards?
options: a: Continually scan the road and roadsides.,b: Stare straight ahead.,c: Rest your left foot on the brake.
note: Safe drivers constantly scan ahead, to the sides, and behind for changing conditions. By checking the road and roadsides, you can spot hazards such as pedestrians, cyclists, animals, or debris early and adjust your speed or position before they become emergencies.

question: What lights should you use when driving in fog?
options: a: Low beam headlights.,b: High beam headlights.,c: Parking lights.
note: In fog, use low beam headlights because their light aims down at the road and is less likely to reflect back at you. High beams can bounce off the fog and reduce your ability to see. Use fog lights if your vehicle has them, along with low beams.

question: When should you always signal?
options: a: When pulling into or out of a parking space.,b: When changing lanes.,c: When pulling into traffic from an alley or parking area.,d: All of the above.
note: You must always signal any time you change where your vehicle is going to move in traffic: when changing lanes, turning, pulling into or out of a parking space, and when entering traffic from an alley, driveway, or parking area. Signaling early and clearly lets other drivers, cyclists, and pedestrians know your intentions so they can adjust and helps prevent crashes.

question: How should you pass another vehicle on a two-lane road with opposite traffic?
options: a: Return to your lane when clear of the passed vehicle.,b: Stay in the left lane if turning left.,c: Return to the right side immediately.
note: On a two-lane road with traffic moving in opposite directions, you must move into the oncoming lane to pass, then return to your original lane only after you are safely ahead of the vehicle you passed and there is enough space. Do not cut back in too soon, and only stay in the left lane if you are actively passing or preparing for a safe left turn where permitted.

question: Which does not promote safe night driving?
options: a: Keep windshield clean.,b: Tinted windows reduce visibility.,c: Carry a flashlight.
note: Safe night driving depends on seeing and being seen clearly. A clean windshield and avoiding dark or heavily tinted windows help reduce glare and improve visibility. Carrying a flashlight may be useful if you stop, but it does not directly improve how safely you drive at night.

question: Which factors influence the effects of alcohol?
options: a: Food in the stomach.,b: Body weight.,c: Time between drinks.,d: All of the above.
note: Food in the stomach slows the absorption of alcohol into the bloodstream, which can lessen how quickly you feel its effects. The overall effect of alcohol also depends on how much you drink, how quickly you drink it, your body weight, and the time between drinks, so two people drinking the same amount may be affected very differently.

question: Is driving under the influence of legally used marijuana legal?
options: a: Legal but not advised.,b: Illegal.,c: Legal.
note: Driving under the influence of marijuana is illegal in all states, even if the marijuana was obtained or used legally. THC impairs judgment, reaction time, and perception, making it unsafe and unlawful to drive.

question: Alcohol/Drug related offenses stay on your record for:
options: a: 5 years.,b: Life.,c: 3 years.,d: 10 years.
note: How long an alcohol- or drug-related offense stays on your driving record varies by state. Some states keep DUI convictions on the record for 10 years, others for longer, and some effectively treat them as permanent. Because there is no single nationwide rule that they always stay on your record for life, you must check your specific state’s law or your state’s driver handbook.

question: How does alcohol affect your ability to drive?
options: a: Even a tiny amount of alcohol can impair concentration, perception, judgment, and memory.,b: Only a blood alcohol level above the legal limit impacts driving ability.,c: Alcohol has no effect on driving skills.
note: Alcohol begins to affect your driving ability with the very first drink. Even a small amount can reduce concentration, slow your reactions, and impair judgment and perception, which are all critical for safe driving. You should never assume you can drive safely after drinking just because you are under the legal limit.

question: What can impair a person's ability to drive?
options: a: Lack of sleep.,b: Certain medications.,c: All of the above.
note: Both lack of sleep and certain medications can seriously impair driving ability by slowing reaction time, reducing coordination, and affecting judgment. Always read medication labels, follow medical advice, and avoid driving when drowsy or under the influence of any substance that affects alertness.

question: How can you ensure your physical condition doesn't impair safe driving?
options: a: Stay physically fit and get regular medical checkups.,b: Know how prescription and over‑the‑counter medications affect your driving.,c: Drive only when you feel well and within your physical limits.,d: All of the above.
note: Safe driving depends on your physical and mental condition. Stay physically fit and get regular checkups, know how any medications you take can affect alertness, vision, or coordination, and always drive within your physical limits so you can react quickly and control the vehicle safely.

question: You arrive at a 4-way stop at the same time as a driver on your left. Who has the right of way?
options: a:The driver on your left, because they were there first,b:You have the right of way — the driver to your left must yield to you,c:Whoever signals first proceeds first,d:The driver going straight always has priority
note: At a 4-way stop when two vehicles arrive simultaneously, the driver to the RIGHT has the right of way. Since the other driver is to your LEFT, you are to their right — meaning you have the right of way and should proceed first.

question: If you must make an emergency stop on an interstate, what should you do?
options: a:Get out of your vehicle and flag down the first vehicle that passes.,b:Pull off the road, turn on your emergency flashers, and stay in your vehicle, if you can.,c:Sound your horn at passing cars to get their attention.
note: If you must stop on an interstate, pull completely off the travel lanes onto the shoulder if possible, turn on your emergency flashers so others can see you, and stay inside your vehicle with your seat belt fastened unless there is an immediate danger such as fire or traffic striking your vehicle.

question: When preparing to pass on a two-lane road, what should be your primary check?
options: a:Judge the distance and speed of oncoming vehicles.,b:Flash your headlights as you pass.,c:Sound your horn as you pass.,d:Assume oncoming traffic will slow down.
note: Before passing on a two-lane road, your main concern is whether there is enough clear space ahead in the oncoming lane. Carefully judge the distance and speed of oncoming vehicles and only begin passing if you are sure you can complete the maneuver and return to your lane without forcing any other driver to slow or swerve.

question: On which road marking may you legally pass another vehicle?
options: a:You are on a road with a solid line next to your lane.,b:You are on a hill or curve.,c:You are on a road with a broken line next to your lane.
note: A broken center line next to your lane means you may pass when it is safe. A solid line next to your lane means you must not pass, and you should never pass on hills, curves, or anywhere your view of oncoming traffic is limited.

question: After passing another vehicle, you should move back into your original lane when:
options: a:You have cleared the front bumper of the passed vehicle.,b:You can see the passed vehicle’s headlights in your rearview mirror.,c:You are 50 feet ahead of the passed vehicle.,d:The passing vehicle signals you to move over.
note: After passing, do not move back into your original lane until you can see the front of the vehicle you passed (its headlights in the daytime or at night) in your rearview mirror. This ensures you have enough space ahead and do not cut off the other driver.

question: What do blue traffic signs generally indicate?
options: a:Regulatory requirements like speed limits.,b:Mileage distances to locations.,c:Construction and maintenance warnings.,d:Information on motorist services (rest areas, hospitals, food).
note: Blue traffic signs are service signs. They give information about motorist services such as rest areas, gas stations, food, lodging, and hospitals along the roadway.

question: When entering a freeway, how should you check traffic to merge safely?
options: a:Using your side mirror and looking over your shoulder.,b:Using only your rearview mirror.,c:Using your rearview and side mirrors without looking over your shoulder.
note: Before merging onto a freeway, use your mirrors and then look over your shoulder to check your blind spot. This helps you see vehicles that are not visible in your mirrors so you can choose a safe gap and merge smoothly.

question: If a child is about to run into the street, what should you do?
options: a:Sound a sharp blast of your horn while being prepared to stop.,b:Flash your headlights.,c:Continue at the same speed.
note: If a child appears ready to run into the street, immediately cover the brake and be prepared to stop while giving a sharp blast of your horn to warn the child and others nearby. Use the horn to alert, but your primary responsibility is to slow or stop to avoid a collision.

question: What must you do when approaching a pedestrian who uses a guide dog or white cane?
options: a:Honk so they know to clear the way.,b:Swerve quickly around them.,c:Yield the right-of-way.
note: Stop and give the blind pedestrian the right-of-way; do not honk or attempt to steer around them abruptly.

question: Alcohol is classified as which type of substance?
options: a:A depressant.,b:A stimulant.,c:An antihistamine.
note: Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant. It slows brain activity and impairs judgment, coordination, and reaction time, making it dangerous to drive after drinking.

question: Any amount of alcohol in your blood may affect which abilities?
options: a:Right-of-way privileges.,b:Judgment and physical coordination.,c:Knowledge.
note: Any amount of alcohol can affect your judgment and physical coordination, even if you do not feel drunk. Because driving requires quick decisions and precise control, even small amounts of alcohol can make driving unsafe.

question: When is using your horn appropriate?
options: a:When it may help prevent a collision.,b:When another driver makes a mistake.,c:When another vehicle is in your way and you want them to move.
note: Use your horn only to alert others to a potential collision or to warn of immediate danger. Do not use it to show anger, impatience, or to punish other drivers for mistakes.

question: Where is it safe to pass another vehicle?
options: a:Where signs and pavement markings indicate passing is permitted and it is safe.,b:Within an intersection if no oncoming vehicles are present.,c:On a curve if you can see ahead a short distance.,d:Anywhere if you signal before passing.
note: Passing is only safe and legal where signs and pavement markings allow it and you have enough clear space to pass without speeding or cutting back in too closely. Never pass in intersections, on curves, or where your view is blocked by hills or other obstacles.

question: At a crosswalk, who has the right-of-way?
options: a:Construction workers must yield to you.,b:You must yield to pedestrians.,c:Pedestrians must yield to you.
note: Drivers must yield to pedestrians in crosswalks, whether marked or unmarked, when pedestrians are in or approaching your lane. Always be prepared to stop for people crossing the street.

question: What does a green arrow signal require you to do?
options: a:Proceed immediately without yielding.,b:Ignore any pedestrians in the intersection.,c:Wait four seconds before proceeding.,d:Yield to vehicles, bicyclists, and pedestrians in the intersection, then complete the turn.
note: A green arrow gives you a protected movement in the direction of the arrow, but you must still yield to any vehicles, bicyclists, or pedestrians already in the intersection before you complete your turn.

question: Why is winter driving more hazardous than other seasons?
options: a:There are increased hours of darkness.,b:Road conditions can be affected by freezing temperatures, ice, snow, and fog.,c:Both of the above.
note: Winter driving is more dangerous because there are more hours of darkness and road surfaces can become slippery or obscured by ice, snow, and fog. These conditions reduce traction and visibility, requiring slower speeds and greater following distances.

question: What general attitude should a driver have about right-of-way rules?
options: a:Assume most drivers obey the right-of-way rules.,b:Always be prepared to yield the right-of-way.,c:Assume all drivers automatically obey the right-of-way rules.
note: Right-of-way laws say who should go first, but they do not guarantee that others will follow them. Safe drivers always stay ready to yield, even when they legally have the right-of-way, if yielding will prevent a collision.

question: When you see a school crossing sign, what should you do?
options: a:Always sound your horn when you see children.,b:Watch for children and be ready to stop.,c:Always stop, whether there is a stop sign or not.
note: A school crossing sign warns that children may be crossing the road. You should slow down, scan carefully for children, and be prepared to stop if they are in or near the crosswalk. You do not automatically stop unless required by a stop sign, signal, or pedestrians in the crosswalk.

question: If a tire blows out suddenly while you're driving, what steps should you take?
options: a:Hold the steering wheel firmly, ease off the accelerator, and exit the traffic lane slowly.,b:Pump the brakes rapidly to stop quickly.,c:Brake hard and steer immediately to the right edge.,d:Turn on your hazards and speed up to reach the shoulder faster.
note: When a tire blows out, the car may pull to one side. Hold the steering wheel firmly, ease off the accelerator, and let the vehicle slow down. Once it is under control and speed has dropped, steer gradually off the road and brake gently if needed. Sudden hard braking or sharp steering can cause loss of control.

question: How many alcoholic drinks does it take to affect your driving ability?
options: a:One,b:Two,c:Three
note: Alcohol begins to affect judgment and reaction time with the first drink. Even one drink can impair your ability to drive safely, so the safest choice is not to drive after drinking any amount of alcohol.

question: What is the only thing that can reduce blood alcohol concentration (BAC)?
options: a:Time,b:Eating foods high in fat,c:Drinking caffeine
note: Once alcohol is in your system, only time allows your body to metabolize it and lower your BAC. Food, coffee, cold showers, or exercise may make you feel more awake but do not speed up the elimination of alcohol.

question: When ridden on public roadways, bicycles are legally classified as:
options: a:Pedestrians.,b:Vehicles.,c:Hazards.,d:Motor vehicles.
note: Bicycles ridden on public roads are treated as vehicles. Cyclists must obey traffic signals, signs, lane markings, and right‑of‑way rules just like drivers of cars, including stopping at red lights and stop signs and riding in the same direction as traffic.

question: If your vehicle has a two-part seat belt, how should you wear it?
options: a:Use only the shoulder belt.,b:Use both the lap and shoulder belts.,c:Use only the lap belt.
note: If your vehicle has both a lap belt and a shoulder belt, you must wear both. The lap belt should be low and snug across the hips, and the shoulder belt should cross the chest and shoulder, not the neck or under the arm. Using only one part greatly reduces protection in a crash.

question: Where is a U-turn prohibited?
options: a:On a straight roadway with a clear view for 500 feet in both directions.,b:On or near any curve or hill.,c:In a parking lot.
note: You must not make a U‑turn on or near a curve or hill where you cannot see far enough ahead to be sure it is safe. Limited visibility makes it hard to judge oncoming traffic and can lead to serious head‑on collisions.

question: Driving noticeably slower than surrounding traffic is:
options: a:Often a hazard because other drivers may become frustrated and try to pass you.,b:Appropriate if you don’t know the speed limit.,c:A good idea if the weather is bad, but you must not drive so slowly that you unnecessarily block or endanger other traffic.
note: Driving much slower than the normal flow of traffic can be dangerous because other drivers may not expect it and may make sudden or risky lane changes or passing maneuvers. You should generally travel at the speed of traffic (within the speed limit) and adjust your speed reasonably for conditions, such as bad weather, without becoming an unnecessary obstruction.

question: What qualifies as a driving distraction?
options: a:Anything that causes evasive action while driving.,b:Anything that takes your attention away from driving.,c:Anything that causes you to pay more attention to driving.
note: A driving distraction is anything that takes your attention away from the driving task—your eyes from the road, your mind from driving, or your hands from the wheel. Examples include texting, eating, adjusting controls, or focusing on passengers instead of traffic.

question: When following another vehicle at night, what headlight setting should you use?
options: a:Keep your headlights on the low beam setting.,b:Use your high beam headlights.,c:Use your high beam headlights until you are within 10 feet of the vehicle ahead.
note: Use low beam headlights when following another vehicle at night so you do not shine bright light into the driver’s mirrors and eyes. High beams can blind or distract the driver ahead, increasing the risk of a crash.

question: What does a double solid yellow centerline indicate?
options: a:Both lanes may pass.,b:The lane to the right may pass.,c:Neither lane may pass.
note: A double solid yellow centerline separates traffic moving in opposite directions and means passing is not allowed from either direction. You may cross these lines only to turn left into or out of a driveway or side road when it is safe.

question: When you want to change lanes, which action should you never do?
options: a:Move into another lane while within an intersection.,b:Check your blind spot by looking over your shoulder.,c:Check for other drivers moving into the same lane.
note: You should not change lanes while you are in an intersection because traffic movements are more complex and other drivers may not expect a lane change there. Instead, change lanes before or after the intersection, and always check mirrors, blind spots, and signal first.

question: If your wheels drop off the pavement edge, what should you do to re-enter safely?
options: a:Wait until it is safe to do so, then gradually re-enter the roadway.,b:Turn back onto the roadway immediately.,c:Stop.
note: If your wheels drop off the pavement, stay calm, ease off the accelerator, and keep a firm grip on the wheel. When traffic allows, gently steer back onto the pavement at a shallow angle. Do not jerk the wheel or brake hard, as that can cause you to lose control.

question: Which headlights should you use to improve visibility in rain or fog?
options: a:High beam headlights.,b:Low beam headlights.,c:Parking lights.
note: In rain, fog, snow, or sleet, use low beam headlights. High beams reflect off moisture in the air and can create glare, making it harder to see. Low beams help you see the road and help other drivers see you without excessive glare.

question: Which driving skills are impaired by alcohol or drug use?
options: a:Alertness.,b:Coordination.,c:Both of the above.
note: Alcohol and many drugs slow your reaction time and make it harder to stay alert and coordinate steering, braking, and acceleration. Because both alertness and coordination are affected, your overall ability to drive safely is reduced.

question: What is the law regarding posters and signs on car windows?
options: a:Are a fun way to personalize your vehicle.,b:Are prohibited by state law if they obstruct a driver's view of the road.,c:Are allowed only if they do not contain offensive language.
note: State law prohibits placing signs or materials on vehicle windows that obstruct the driver's clear view of the roadway.

question: A flashing yellow light at an intersection tells you to:
options: a:Slow down and proceed with caution.,b:Come to a complete stop as quickly as possible.,c:Stop and proceed only when the intersection is clear.
note: A flashing yellow light warns you to slow down and proceed through the intersection with caution. You do not have to stop unless needed for other traffic, pedestrians, or to avoid a hazard.

question: How do you drive defensively?
options: a:Put one car length between you and the car ahead.,b:Look only at the car in front of you while driving.,c:Keep your eyes moving to look for possible hazards.
note: Defensive driving means constantly scanning the road ahead, behind, and to the sides so you can spot potential hazards early. By keeping your eyes moving and checking mirrors, you have more time to react and avoid collisions.

question: Before switching on the ignition, what safety checks should you perform?
options: a:Be sure all passengers have buckled their safety belts.,b:Buckle your safety belt.,c:Both of the above.
note: Before starting the vehicle, you should always buckle your own seat belt and make sure all passengers are properly buckled. This simple habit greatly reduces the risk of injury in a crash.

question: A pedestrian starts crossing after the \Don't Walk\" signal begins flashing and is in the middle of the street when your light turns green. What should you do?"
options: a:Proceed if the pedestrian is not in your lane.,b:Wait until the pedestrian finishes crossing before proceeding.,c:Proceed since you have the green and the pedestrian is mid-street.,d:Honk to make the pedestrian hurry.
note: If a pedestrian is in the intersection when your light turns green, allow them to finish crossing before you proceed.

question: You should avoid using your horn when driving near:
options: a:Drivers whose visibility ahead is limited.,b:Blind pedestrians.,c:Vehicles about to collide with you.,d:Pedestrians in crosswalks at night.
note: You should not use your horn around blind pedestrians because they rely heavily on sound cues to understand traffic movement. A sudden horn blast can be confusing or frightening. Instead, slow down, yield, and pass only when it is clearly safe.

question: Reaction time is slower after which of the following?
options: a:Drinking alcohol.,b:Sleeping.,c:Working hard.
note: Alcohol slows your brain’s processing and your body’s reflexes, so it takes longer to notice hazards and react. Even small amounts of alcohol can increase reaction time and reduce your ability to drive safely.

question: Which factor listed affects how alcohol is absorbed into the body?
options: a:Height,b:Weight,c:Intelligence
note: Body weight is one of the main factors that affects how alcohol is absorbed and how strongly it affects you. In general, a smaller person will reach a higher blood alcohol concentration than a larger person after drinking the same amount.

question: Which road surface is most likely to freeze first?
options: a:A tunnel,b:An intersection,c:A bridge
note: Bridges and overpasses freeze first because cold air can circulate above and below the surface, causing them to cool more quickly than regular roadways that sit on the ground.

question: If you are already within an intersection when a green light changes to yellow, what should you do?
options: a:Continue moving and clear the intersection safely.,b:Stop.,c:Increase your speed so as not to cause an accident.
note: If the light turns yellow after you have already entered the intersection, you should continue through and clear the intersection safely. Stopping suddenly in the intersection can cause rear‑end collisions and block cross traffic.

question: If a tire suddenly goes flat while driving, what should you do?
options: a:Turn sharply toward the nearest shoulder.,b:Grip the wheel firmly, slow down gradually without heavy braking, and pull off when safe.,c:Rapidly pump the brake pedal several times.,d:Press the brake pedal as hard as possible immediately.
note: When a tire blows out or goes flat, hold the steering wheel firmly, keep the vehicle going straight, ease off the accelerator, and let the vehicle slow down gradually. Avoid hard braking, then steer to the shoulder and stop in a safe place.

question: Approaching an intersection controlled by a flashing red traffic signal, what must you do?
options: a:Come to a complete stop, yield to oncoming traffic or pedestrians, then proceed.,b:Reduce your speed and proceed with caution.,c:Come to a complete stop and remain stopped as long as the light is red.
note: A flashing red light is treated like a stop sign. You must come to a complete stop, look for and yield to any traffic or pedestrians, and then proceed only when it is safe.

question: When is highway pavement especially slippery?
options: a:If it has just begun to rain.,b:If it has been raining several hours.,c:If it has been raining for one to two hours.
note: Roads are often most slippery just after it starts to rain because oil and other residues on the road surface mix with the water and create a slick film before being washed away.

question: When driving on gravel or dirt roads, how does traction compare to pavement and what should you do?
options: a:Traction is the same as pavement under all conditions.,b:Visibility is always better than on pavement, so speed is fine.,c:Your tires grip better than on pavement, so maintain speed.,d:You have less traction than on pavement, so slow down.
note: On gravel or dirt roads, your tires have less traction than on paved roads, so it is easier to skid and it takes longer to stop. You should slow down and allow extra space for stopping and turning.

question: What is the purpose of broken yellow lines on the roadway?
options: a:Separate lanes of traffic moving in opposite directions.,b:Indicate no passing zones.,c:Separate lanes of traffic moving in the same direction.
note: Broken (dashed) yellow center lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions and indicate that passing is allowed when it can be done safely and legally. Solid yellow lines, or solid with broken, are used to mark no-passing or restricted-passing zones.

question: If another vehicle is passing you, you should:
options: a:Brake hard to make the pass quicker.,b:Maintain a constant speed and allow the vehicle to pass safely.,c:Speed up to prevent the pass.,d:Move into the passing lane immediately.
note: When another vehicle is passing you, stay in your lane and maintain a steady, safe speed so the other driver can complete the pass quickly and safely. Do not speed up or brake suddenly, as that can create a dangerous situation.

question: When is it best to change from one lane to another?
options: a:Quickly and often.,b:When a car is in your blind spot.,c:Gradually and carefully.
